steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing a functional, Bayesian version of Tucker decomposition for tensor data with continuous indexes. Explain tensor decomposition, why it breaks for continuous-indexed data, the gaps in existing approaches, and then summarize our method and results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Tensor decomposition and its uses
- Limitation: discrete, finite modes vs. continuous-indexed data
- Existing workarounds and their gaps
- Our method: FunBaT, and evaluation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Tensor decomposition
  - analyze/predict multi-way or multi-aspect data
  - medical records: four-mode tensor (patients, doctor, clinics, time), values visit count or drug usage
  - weather: (latitude, longitude, time), values temperature
  - low-rank representations per mode (factors), estimated to reconstruct observed entries
  - models: CP (cite), tensor train (cite), Tucker (cite) widely used for capacity, flexibility, interpretability
- Limitation
  - data must be structured grids; each mode discrete, finite-dimensional
  - finite set of objects indexed by integers (user 1, user 2, …); entries located by tuple of discrete indexes
  - climate/geographic modeling: continuous coordinates (latitude, longitude, time); tuple of continuous indexes; can't apply directly
- Workarounds
  - discretize modes: bin timestamps into steps (weeks, months), bin latitude into ranges numbered 1, 2, 3…
  - loses fine-grained info, hard to choose discretization (cite)
  - more natural: extend tensor models from grid to continuous field
  - existing: tensor-train (cite) or simpler CP (cite); not Tucker
  - mostly deterministic, polynomial approximations, no probabilistic inference, poor on noisy incomplete data
- FunBaT
  - Functional Bayesian Tucker decomposition; Tucker generalized to functional field, probabilistic
  - Tucker core x latent functions mapping continuous indexes to mode-wise factors
  - functions as GPs; state-space priors via equivalent SDEs to cut cost, following prior work (cite)
  - inference: conditional expectation propagation (CEP) (cite) + Bayesian filter for posterior of factors
  - also extends CP to continuous-indexed data (simplified setting)
  - experiments: synthetic + real-world climate modeling; beats SOTA by large margins in reconstruction error; interpretable patterns matching domain knowledge

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Tensor decomposition is widely used to analyze and predict with multi-way or multi-aspect data in real-world applications. For example, medical service records can be put into a four-mode tensor (patients, doctor, clinics, time), and the entry values can be the visit count or the drug usage. Weather data can be represented by tensors like (latitude, longitude, time), and the entry values can be the temperature. Tensor decomposition introduces a set of low-rank representations of the objects in each mode, called factors, and it estimates these factors to reconstruct the observed entry values. Many tensor decomposition models have been proposed, like CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) decomposition and tensor train (TT), and Tucker decomposition is widely-used because of its fair capacity, flexibility and interpretability.

But the standard tensor decomposition framework has a fundamental limitation. It restricts the data format to structured grids, and it requires each mode of the tensor to be discrete and finite-dimensional. This means each mode has a finite set of objects that are indexed by integers, such as user 1, user 2, …, and each entry value is located by the tuple of discrete indexes. However, in many real-world applications like climate and geographic modeling, the data is represented with continuous coordinates of modes, e.g., latitude, longitude and time. Here each data entry is located by a tuple of continuous indexes, so tensor decomposition cannot be applied directly.

- Workarounds and gaps
  - discretize modes: bin timestamps (weeks, months), bin latitude into ranges numbered 1, 2, 3…
  - fine-grained info lost, discretization strategy hard to pick
  - extend models from grid to continuous field: existing methods only tensor-train or simpler CP, not Tucker
  - mostly deterministic, polynomial approximations; no probabilistic inference; noisy, incomplete data hard
- FunBaT (Functional Bayesian Tucker decomposition)
  - Tucker core + latent functions mapping continuous indexes to mode-wise factors
  - GPs, converted to state-space priors via equivalent SDEs (following prior work)
  - inference: CEP framework + Bayesian filter for factor posteriors
  - also covers CP with simplified setting
  - synthetic + real-world climate data; large margins in reconstruction error; interpretable patterns

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Tensor decomposition is widely used to analyze and predict with multi-way or multi-aspect data in real-world applications. For example, medical service records can be put into a four-mode tensor (patients, doctor, clinics, time), and the entry values can be the visit count or the drug usage. Weather data can be represented by tensors like (latitude, longitude, time), and the entry values can be the temperature. Tensor decomposition introduces a set of low-rank representations of the objects in each mode, called factors, and it estimates these factors to reconstruct the observed entry values. Many tensor decomposition models have been proposed, like CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) decomposition and tensor train (TT), and Tucker decomposition is widely-used because of its fair capacity, flexibility and interpretability.

But the standard tensor decomposition framework has a fundamental limitation. It restricts the data format to structured grids, and it requires each mode of the tensor to be discrete and finite-dimensional. This means each mode has a finite set of objects that are indexed by integers, such as user 1, user 2, …, and each entry value is located by the tuple of discrete indexes. However, in many real-world applications like climate and geographic modeling, the data is represented with continuous coordinates of modes, e.g., latitude, longitude and time. Here each data entry is located by a tuple of continuous indexes, so tensor decomposition cannot be applied directly.

One widely-used trick to make tensor models work on such data is to discretize the modes. For example, the timestamps are binned into time steps (say, by weeks or months), or the latitude values are binned into a set of ranges, and the ranges are numbered 1, 2, 3… This is feasible, but the fine-grained information is lost, and in many cases it is hard to decide on a good discretization strategy. A more natural solution is to extend tensor models from grid-structure to continuous field. As far as we know, most existing methods in this direction are limited to tensor-train or the simpler CP format, and they cannot be applied to Tucker decomposition, which is an important compact and flexible low-rank representation. Also, most of the proposed methods are deterministic and use polynomial approximations, so they cannot provide probabilistic inference and have a hard time handling noisy, incomplete data.

To bridge this gap, we propose FunBaT: Fun ctional Ba yesian T ucker decomposition, which generalizes the standard Tucker decomposition to the functional field in a probabilistic framework. We decompose the continuous-indexed tensor data as the interaction between the Tucker core and a group of latent functions, and these functions map the continuous indexes to mode-wise factors. We approximate the functions with Gaussian processes (GPs). To reduce the computational cost, we follow prior work and convert them into state-space priors by constructing equivalent stochastic differential equations (SDE). Then we develop an efficient inference algorithm, based on the conditional expectation propagation (CEP) framework and the Bayesian filter, that approximates the posterior distribution of the factors. We show that this framework can also extend CP decomposition to continuous-indexed data with a simplified setting. We did experiments on both synthetic data and real-world applications of climate modeling for evaluation. The results show that FunBaT outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by large margins in reconstruction error, and that it also finds interpretable patterns that align with domain knowledge.

steps.text:

A more natural solution is to extend tensor models from grid-structure to continuous field. As far as we know, most existing methods in this direction are limited to tensor-train [5,6,7,8] or the simpler CP format [9], and they cannot be applied to Tucker decomposition, which is an important compact and flexible low-rank representation. Also, most of the proposed methods are deterministic and use polynomial approximations, so they cannot provide probabilistic inference and have a hard time handling noisy, incomplete data.

To bridge this gap, we propose FunBaT: Fun ctional Ba yesian T ucker decomposition, which generalizes the standard Tucker decomposition to the functional field in a probabilistic framework. steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Tensor decomposition is widely used to analyze and predict with multi-way or multi-aspect data in real-world applications. For example, medical service records can be summarized by a four-mode tensor (patients, doctor, clinics, time), with the visit count or drug usage as entry values. Weather data can be abstracted by tensors like (latitude, longitude, time), with the temperature as entry values. Tensor decomposition introduces a set of low-rank representations of objects in each mode, known as factors, and estimates these factors to reconstruct the observed entry values. Among the numerous proposed tensor decomposition models, such as CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) [1] decomposition and tensor train (TT) [2], Tucker decomposition [3] is widely-used for its fair capacity, flexibility and interpretability.

Despite its success, the standard tensor decomposition framework has a fundamental limitation: it restricts the data format to structured grids, and demands that each mode of the tensor be discrete and finite-dimensional. That is, each mode includes a finite set of objects indexed by integers, such as user 1, user 2, …, and each entry value is located by a tuple of discrete indexes. However, in many real-world applications like climate and geographic modeling, the data is represented as continuous coordinates of modes, e.g., latitude, longitude and time. In these cases, each data entry is located by a tuple of continuous indexes, and tensor decomposition cannot be applied directly.

To enable tensor models on such data, one widely-used trick is to discretize the modes, for example, binning the timestamps into time steps (say, by weeks or months), or binning the latitude values into a set of ranges numbered 1, 2, 3… While feasible, this loses the fine-grained information, and it is hard to decide on an appropriate discretization strategy in many cases [4]. A more natural solution is to extend tensor models from grid-structure to continuous field. To the best of our knowledge, most existing methods in that direction are limited to tensor-train [5,6,7,8] or the simpler CP format [9], and cannot be applied to Tucker decomposition, an important compact and flexible low-rank representation. Moreover, most of the proposed methods are deterministic with polynomial approximations, cannot provide probabilistic inference, and struggle to handle noisy, incomplete data.

To bridge the gap, we propose FunBaT: Fun ctional Ba yesian T ucker decomposition, which generalizes the standard Tucker decomposition to the functional field under a probabilistic framework. We decompose the continuous-indexed tensor data as the interaction between the Tucker core and a group of latent functions that map the continuous indexes to mode-wise factors. We approximate these functions by Gaussian processes (GPs), and follow [10] to convert them into state-space priors by constructing equivalent stochastic differential equations (SDE), which reduces the computational cost. We then develop an efficient inference algorithm based on the conditional expectation propagation (CEP) framework [11] and Bayesian filter to approximate the posterior distribution of the factors. We show that this framework can also extend CP decomposition to continuous-indexed data in a simplified setting. For evaluation, we conducted experiments on both synthetic data and real-world applications of climate modeling. The results show that FunBaT not only outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by large margins in reconstruction error, but also identifies interpretable patterns aligned with domain knowledge.
